b: When I began writing my second poetry collection, Future Tense, a memoir in verse, I wanted it to be the one thing I rarely hear collections called: a page-turner.

The book documents the three years I fought to become a mom while losing my own, ending with my daughter’s adoption shortly before my mom’s death. Because life was changing minute by minute, diagnosis by diagnosis, I knew the book could unfold that way too.

I wanted to build a collection that pulled readers forward—not because they needed to know what happened next, but because they needed to know what the next poem would reveal. Each poem would deepen the tangled story, creating the emotional momentum of a novel. I wanted to make readers look up to realize they’d just devoured fifty pages of poetry.

Because poetry can do this. It can move fast and deep, ask us to feel before we understand, and hold contradiction, mystery, and hard truths at once. And yet poetry has a reputation for being difficult—a slog you have to wade through rather than something you can’t wait to keep reading.
With Future Tense, I wanted to take my lifelong mission of expanding what poetry can do one step further: to show that genre doesn’t define momentum.
Here are five craft approaches, along with the questions I asked myself, for creating a poetry collection that reads with urgency and momentum.
What Makes a Story Worth Following?

Story sticks—it’s the emotional architecture through which we view the world: what the speaker wants, what stands in her way, and what’s at stake. Plot is the specific sequence of events that forces her through those obstacles.
This is what makes collections like Fixer by Edgar Kunz and Stag’s Leap by Sharon Olds linger: they anchor us in a specific event with clear stakes, then show how the speaker navigates and changes.
When I ordered Future Tense, I wanted the first poems to promise a story. I used “A Maybe, A Yes, a Not” to show that I wanted a baby, but that we had already been trying for some time:

The gaps. I measure. I math. Worn by wait.
The coats, the labs: hint age, test rot: ovaries,
Eggs. A maybe, yes, then not.
We lose. We gain. Try again. Bury names.
An almost-boy, a close call-girl, two weeks
then no. I hoard my hope. Tread time to cope.
I wanted to drop the reader in medias res, into immediate conflict. The speaker isn’t at the start of the journey but already in the mess. The book promises no answers, only tension.

In “Late,” I show my mom, newly moved from New Jersey to California, excited for her future grandchildren—and the life she rearranged to share with us. But the final line foreshadows something darker: “Does the future ever arrive in the dress we pick out?”
Two poems later, my mother is diagnosed with Stage Four cancer. Suddenly, the future the speaker imagined is slipping away.
Two stories and conflicts unfold at once, leaving the reader with one question: Will the speaker become a mother before her mother dies? That question becomes the book’s spine.
How Do You Build a Book That Moves?
Structure—the way a book is put together and its poems are packaged—can make a collection feel both innovative and inevitable.

Think of Victoria Chang’s Obit, where each poem functions as an obituary for the human and nonhuman, literal and abstract; Caitlin Conlon’s Burning the Ghostlight, poetry written as a four-act play; or Matt Rasmussen’s Black Aperture, where the speaker relives the day after his brother’s suicide from different angles. In each, structure and form deepen the content, adding another layer of story and another facet of what the book is arguing.
Throughout Future Tense, I used structure to create forward momentum and make the book feel like a countdown. As time accumulates, so does pressure; as grief deepens, time both adds and subtracts.

Future Tense follows a traditional three-act narrative structure. I knew I needed an inciting incident—a one-way door the speaker walks through—along with rising conflict and tension. I also needed propulsion, so I carefully placed revealing poems and juxtaposed apparent resolutions with new, deeper complications.
Each section begins and ends on a cliffhanger and is named for a measurement of time: Six Months In, One Year In, Two Years In, and so on. Time becomes a countdown, an antagonist.
What Can Be Lost—and What Are You Withholding?
Stakes are what can be lost—and tension is the distance between what the reader wants to know and what you are willing to tell them.

In Writing the Breakout Novel, Donald Maass argues that a book needs conflict on every page to remain propulsive. Poetry collections need a similar sense of consequence. Each poem should have a specific function: showing why what’s happening matters and how it complicates what came before.

I wanted readers to know what the speaker had to lose—and what she was willing to risk. As the stakes rose, I tracked every storyline in a spreadsheet: each character’s arc, when information was revealed, where emotional peaks landed, and how pressure accumulated.

In Future Tense, my mother is diagnosed with Stage Four cancer while I’m struggling with infertility. Her dying wish is to become a grandmother—a wish I cannot grant her. Then my marriage begins to unravel. We cannot conceive and cannot agree on how to make a family from our heartache.

In the title poem, the speaker fights with her husband about waiting to see if they can get pregnant, but she doesn’t want to wait. “The cost of anything is how long you’ll wait.” The question wasn’t simply, Will she become a mother? But what will it cost her to become one?

At times, it feels like she must choose between marriage and motherhood. The second section ends with “Year of Thirst,” where she tells her husband, “I’m moving forward with adoption…With or without you.” The poem ends with the river forking: “No telling if it will find itself again.”
But stakes alone aren’t enough. Poems should earn the next page—changing what we understand, sharpening the questions we need answered, or withholding what we’re desperate to know.

Tension can come through information, emotion, or form. In “What I Wish I Could Say to My Daughter’s Birthmom,” I used strike-throughs to show hesitation and the struggle to say the most honest things aloud—both gratitude and hurt.
What I Wish I Could Say to My Daughter’s Birth Mother

I know what it’s like to go home empty. To harbor a version of yourself
you cannot keep. In the white-walled hospital, we wept. You: refusing
to hold her. Me: sick with what I couldn’t carry. How she belonged to both
and neither of us. So grateful (jealous) of one another’s luck.

One of my favorite sources of tension is interiority—the chance to live inside another person’s heart and mind. Once inside, the reader knows what other characters don’t. I wanted to give the reader access to places filled with silence, stigma, and shame: waiting rooms and bedrooms, dinner table conversations, and the silences where the hardest things couldn’t be said. And the pain of watching the world recreate and grow something new when you no longer can.

Everything hurts: wildflowers
on the freeway, beached
kelp wild with wind, a sea
otter drunk on a mother’s
warmth. This world keeps
remaking itself—without me.

I oar alone. I stare
at the horizon, gray
as oyster meat.

I wanted to show that infertility is so much more than I really want a baby. It tests everything you know about yourself: how you define family and love, and how much you need to control each. It creates financial, body, and emotional tension.
In “A Fertility Clinic Is the Coldest Place on Earth” I write,
When will you fail yourself / again / It’s so easy for some / and others $50K later / $100K later / You can’t afford to be here To want
In “My Mother Asks About Adoption,” my mother’s health was declining, increasing the pressure and raising the stakes.

Maybe next year, I interrupt, thinking only of my own ruin. If I don’t save my marriage, there might never be a baby. I don’t consider the cancer choking every organ. Mom nods, softer. It’s just—I won’t be here forever.
The tension came from not knowing how any of it would resolve.
What Has Changed by the End?

Any great piece of art requires movement. As Vivian Gornick says, a narrator must take the reader on a journey, “make the piece arrive,” and ultimately “bring us out into a clearing where the sense of things is larger than it was before.” We need to see something change before our eyes and know how it gets bigger, deeper, more important.

Images need to take on new meaning. Characters reveal things we didn’t expect. By the end of Future Tense, I wanted readers to feel the accumulation of it all—the indentations made by grief and love, not just what each person lost, but what they carried forward. Images such as flowers and sailboats, the ocean and its tide, mean one thing early in the book and something entirely different by the end. They carry new stories.

The speaker changes, and experience reshapes how they define some of their most fundamental beliefs. The ocean represents isolation at the beginning and middle of the collection; in “Infertility,” I write,

There is no land
or other side in sight.
I drown inside
my tiny boat.
I continue
to sink.
I continue
to row.

Throughout the collection, the speakers’ relationship to the ocean transforms in both meaning and significance. In “Dearest Everything,” about the birth of my daughter, that interpretation and meaning shift,

You open your eyes for the first time. Pacific deep.
Iris ringed with indigo. Now, I understand every sea
we needed to cross to call you home.

The speaker’s understanding of motherhood changes; she understands what it takes to fight for it, and how love reshapes itself under pressure. A question that once felt impossible can become a question the speaker is finally willing to live inside.
That, to me, is evolution: not simply that something happened, but that the meaning of what happened changed. This is how the book earns its ending.
And if I’ve done my job, by the time the reader reaches the final page, they don’t just understand what happened; they understand why they had to keep turning the pages to get there.
Future Tense by Kelly Grace Thomas is available from Alice James Books.
